title: Win rate is not profit
summary: Why a bot that wins 99 trades in 100 can still lose money, what expectancy measures, and the large losses behind averaging down and selling crash insurance.

lessons.title: The 99% bot and the 56% bot
body: Trading bots are often sold on their **win rate**: the share of trades that made money. A bot that wins 99 trades in 100 sounds safer than one that wins 56. Win rate alone does not show that.
Win rate counts trades. It says nothing about how much each win made or how much each loss cost. A bot can take many tiny profits and then give them all back, and more, in one bad trade.
The picture shows two made-up bots with $10,000 each. One wins almost every time. The other wins a little more than half the time. Watch what one large loss does.

visual.alt: Two made-up accounts start at $10,000. The 99% bot climbs smoothly with tiny wins and leads for most of the chart, then one loss drops it below its start. The 56% bot climbs in a bumpy line and ends far ahead.

steps.caption: Two made-up bots, $10,000 each. The 99% bot wins small amounts almost every time.
After 150 trades the 99% bot is still close, with a smooth line that looks safe.
One loss wipes out every gain and more. The bot that wins less often ends far ahead.

inParity.label: Glossary: the high win rate myth
Verify: check a bot's trade log for this

check.q: What does a win rate tell you?
options: How much money a strategy made
check.why: Win rate only counts trades. It ignores the size of each win and each loss, so it cannot say how much was made or how risky it was.

check.q: How can a 99% win rate lose money?
options: The rare losses are much larger than all the small wins together
check.why: If each win is tiny and the one loss is huge, the loss can cancel every win and more.

lessons.title: Expectancy: average profit per trade
body: **Expectancy** is what a trade is worth on average. It is the win rate times the average win, minus the loss rate times the average loss. It is the same as adding up every trade and dividing by the number of trades.

Take a made-up bot that wins $10 on 99 trades and loses $1,500 on one. Its expectancy is 0.99 x $10 minus 0.01 x $1,500, which is minus $5.10 a trade. Now take one that wins $100 on 56 trades and loses $80 on 44. Its expectancy is 0.56 x $100 minus 0.44 x $80, which is plus $20.80.
The **profit factor** says the same thing another way: all the money won divided by all the money lost. Under 1 means the strategy loses money overall, whatever its win rate.

visual.alt: Bars compare two made-up bots. Win rate: 99% against 56%. Average loss: $1,500 against $80. Expectancy per trade: minus $5.10 against plus $20.80.

steps.caption: Expectancy per trade: minus $5.10 against plus $20.80. The 56% bot is the one that makes money.

check.q: A bot wins 80% of trades. Its average win is $20 and its average loss is $100. What is its expectancy?
check.why: 0.8 x $20 = $16, and 0.2 x $100 = $20. $16 minus $20 is minus $4 a trade.

check.q: What does a profit factor under 1 mean?
options: The strategy trades less than once a day
check.why: Profit factor is all the money won divided by all the money lost. Under 1, the losses are bigger than the wins.

lessons.title: Doubling down and averaging down
body: A **martingale** bot doubles its bet after every loss. In trading the same idea is **averaging down**: buy more each time the price falls, then sell everything after a small bounce. Almost every cycle ends in a small win, so the win rate is very high.

Each new buy is twice the last. A long fall without a bounce makes the position huge compared with the account. Then the money runs out, or the broker closes everything in a **margin call**, and years of small wins are lost in one trade.
In Parity's Bot Battle, a doubling bot on US stock prices since 1928 won 99% of its trades and still lost most of its money. That is a backtest of a simple rule with past prices, not a prediction.

visual.alt: A made-up account that doubles down climbs in a smooth straight line for most of the chart, winning every trade, then drops close to zero in a single trade near the end.

steps.caption: Made-up example: every cycle ends in a small win. The line rises steadily.
Then one fall without a bounce. The doubling runs out of money and one loss takes almost everything.

inParity.label: Parity Terminal: Bot Battle, US stocks from 1928
Verify: spot a martingale in a trade log

check.q: Why does an averaging-down bot have such a high win rate?
options: It keeps buying until a small bounce turns the whole position into a small win
It only trades on good days
check.why: It never takes a loss voluntarily. It buys more and waits for a bounce, so most cycles end in a small win.

options: A long fall with no bounce, which makes the position too large for the account
check.why: Each buy doubles, so a long enough fall needs more money than the account has, and the whole position is closed at a large loss.

lessons.title: Selling crash insurance
body: Some strategies earn a small, steady fee for taking on a rare large risk. Selling crash insurance is the common example: you are paid a little every week, and you pay out only when prices fall hard. Traders call it picking up pennies in front of a steamroller.
Returns like this have **negative skew**: many small gains and a few very large losses. The calm years make the strategy look safe and its volatility look low, until the crash.
The buyer of that insurance has the opposite shape: many small losses and a rare large win. Its win rate is low, and it can still be the one that ends ahead.

visual.alt: Two made-up accounts. The insurance seller rises steadily with frequent small wins, then drops sharply in one crash. The insurance buyer drifts down with frequent small losses, then jumps up in the same crash.

steps.caption: Made-up example. The seller collects small fees and wins most weeks.
The buyer pays those fees and loses most weeks.
Then a crash. The seller pays out a large sum in one go, and the buyer is paid it.

inParity.label: Parity Terminal: the Picking up pennies bot in Bot Battle

options: Mostly small gains with rare very large losses
check.why: A negatively skewed strategy earns a little most of the time and loses a lot once in a while.

check.q: Why can a smooth record be misleading for this kind of strategy?
options: The large loss may simply not have happened yet in the years measured
Smoothness means the costs were left out
check.why: Years without a crash look calm. The risk is still there, it just has not shown up in that window.

lessons.title: Worst fall and the time to climb back
body: Two more numbers sit next to win rate on Parity's Bot Battle board: the **worst fall** from a high, and how long the account stayed under that high.

Falls and gains are not symmetric. After a 50% fall you need a 100% gain to get back to where you were. After a 90% fall you need 900%. That is why a single large loss matters so much more than many small wins.
Time matters too. An account that spends ten years under its old high has tied up money for a decade, even if it ends ahead. A bot that never recovers shows as "never".

visual.alt: An account rises, falls about 50 percent in a short burst and climbs back slowly. A dashed line marks its highest point so far, and a red area shows the depth of the fall below it.

steps.caption: It falls by about half. The dashed line is its old high.
The red area is the fall. Climbing back from minus 50% takes a 100% gain, and a long time.

inParity.label: Parity Terminal: worst fall and time under water in Bot Battle

check.q: An account falls 50%. What gain gets it back to where it started?
check.why: Half of $10,000 is $5,000. Getting from $5,000 back to $10,000 is a gain of 100%.

check.q: Why can time under water matter even when a strategy ends ahead?
options: Years below an old high tie up money and test whether anyone would keep going
check.why: Long spells below a previous high are hard to sit through, and the money could have been used elsewhere.
